questions.question: Six equal squares are joined edge to edge in one straight row, like a 1-by-6 strip. Which statement about this net is true?
options: It will not fold into a cube: a cube net has at most 4 squares in a row.
It folds into a cube, because any six squares joined edge to edge will close.
It folds into a cube, because a cube has 6 faces and here there are 6 squares.
It will not fold, because a cube needs 8 squares, one square for each corner.
questions.explain: A cube net needs a band of 4 squares wrapping the sides plus a top and a bottom, so a straight strip of 6 can never close up; the trap is thinking any six connected squares make a cube.

questions.question: Sam is drawing a net for a triangular prism. Which set of flat shapes will fold up into that prism?
options: 6 shapes: 2 triangles and 4 rectangles
5 shapes: 2 triangles and 3 rectangles
4 shapes: 1 triangle and 3 rectangles
5 shapes: 3 triangles and 2 rectangles
questions.explain: A triangular prism has 2 triangular ends plus 1 rectangle for each of the 3 base edges, so its net shows 5 faces; the common slip is copying the 6 faces of a rectangular prism.

questions.question: A closed cylinder, like a soup can with both a top and a bottom, is cut open and laid out flat. Which set of pieces is its net?
options: 1 rectangle and 1 circle
2 rectangles and 2 circles
1 rectangle and 2 circles
1 triangle and 2 circles
questions.explain: The curved surface unrolls into one single rectangle and each flat end is a circle, so the net is 1 rectangle plus 2 circles; forgetting one of the two ends is the usual mistake.

questions.question: A net has 6 equal squares: a row of 4 squares, with 1 extra square joined above the 2nd square and 1 extra square joined above the 3rd square. Which statement is true?
options: It folds into a cube, because a row of 4 squares always wraps around and closes.
It will not fold, because no cube net is allowed to have 4 squares in a row.
It folds into a cube, because it is made of 6 squares joined edge to edge.
It will not fold: both extra squares land on top and the bottom stays open.
questions.explain: The row of 4 wraps around the sides, so the two extra squares must sit on opposite sides of that row to cap the top and the bottom; putting both above leaves the bottom open even with 6 squares.

questions.question: Mia carefully cuts open an empty cereal box, which is a rectangular prism, and flattens it out. Which statement about the net she gets is true?
options: It has 6 rectangles that come in 3 matching pairs of equal size.
It has 4 rectangles, since the top and the bottom flaps are not real faces.
It has 8 rectangles, one for each corner where the box is folded.
It has 6 rectangles that are all exactly the same size and shape.
questions.explain: Opposite faces of a rectangular prism are identical, so the net is 6 rectangles forming 3 matching pairs; counting corners or leaving off the top and bottom gives the wrong face count.

questions.question: A closed gift box is a hexagonal prism. How many pieces must its net have, and of what kinds?
options: 7 pieces: 1 hexagon and 6 rectangles
8 pieces: 2 hexagons and 6 rectangles
12 pieces: 6 hexagons and 6 rectangles
6 pieces: 2 hexagons and 4 rectangles
questions.explain: A prism net has one rectangle for every edge of the base plus the 2 base shapes, so a hexagonal prism needs 6 rectangles and 2 hexagons; dropping one base is the usual face-count error.

questions.question: Jayden rolls a rectangle into a tube for a poster mailer, then adds flat circular ends. Which statement about his net is true?
options: The net needs just 1 circle, because a mailer only has one lid on it.
The rolled side of the rectangle must match the diameter of a circle.
The rolled side of the rectangle must match a circle's circumference.
The net needs 3 circles: a lid, a base, and a middle divider piece.
questions.explain: As the rectangle rolls up, its rolling edge becomes the distance around the circle, and each end needs its own circle; matching that edge to the diameter instead is the common trap.

questions.question: Six equal squares are joined into a solid 2-by-3 block, that is 2 rows of 3 squares each. Which statement is true?
options: It folds into a cube, because it uses exactly 6 squares with no gaps.
It folds into a cube, because every square is joined along a full edge.
It will not fold, because a cube needs 7 squares: 6 sides and a lid.
It will not fold: faces overlap and some sides of the cube stay open.
questions.explain: Fold the 2-by-3 block and one row wraps while the other row doubles up, leaving sides open, so it is not a cube net; six squares are necessary but never enough on their own.

questions.question: A chocolate box is a triangular prism 20 cm long, and its triangular end has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm. Which rectangles must appear in the net of this box?
options: Two rectangles 5 cm by 20 cm and one rectangle 6 cm by 20 cm.
Two rectangles 6 cm by 20 cm and one rectangle 5 cm by 20 cm.
Four rectangles, each 5 cm by 20 cm, one for every edge of the end.
Three rectangles, each 5 cm by 20 cm, one per side face.
questions.explain: Each rectangle in a prism net matches one base edge and the length of the prism, so a 5, 5, 6 triangle gives 5 by 20, 5 by 20 and 6 by 20; the trap is making all three rectangles the same.

questions.question: A tomato soup can is 8 cm tall and the distance around its circular lid is 22 cm. Emma unrolls the whole can into a net. Which net is correct?
options: A 22 cm by 16 cm rectangle plus a circle at each end.
A 22 cm by 8 cm rectangle plus a circle at each end.
An 8 cm by 8 cm rectangle plus a circle at each end.
A 22 cm by 8 cm rectangle plus one circle for the lid.
questions.explain: The rectangle's rolling side is the distance around the can, 22 cm, and its other side is the height, 8 cm, and both ends still need a circle; doubling the height for the two ends is a common slip.

questions.question: Noah draws 6 equal squares: a row of 5 squares with 1 extra square joined above the last one. He says it must fold into a cube because it has 6 squares. What is wrong with his thinking?
options: Nothing is wrong; six squares joined edge to edge always close into a cube.
He is wrong, because a cube is built from 6 rectangles and not from squares.
He is wrong: a row of 5 cannot wrap, since the band takes only 4 squares.
He is wrong, because a cube net needs 8 squares, one for each of its corners.
questions.explain: Only 4 squares can form the band that wraps around a cube, so a row of 5 already overlaps itself; having 6 squares is necessary, but the arrangement decides whether the net folds.

questions.question: Priya builds a display case from a flat pattern of 2 identical pentagons and 5 equal rectangles, with the rectangles in a band and one pentagon capping each end. What has she made?
options: A pentagonal prism, but the pattern is short by 2 more rectangles.
A pentagonal prism, which really needs 10 faces, one per edge.
A pentagonal pyramid, and 5 plus 1 gives the 6 faces it needs.
A pentagonal prism, and 5 plus 2 gives the 7 faces it needs.
questions.explain: A prism band has one rectangle per base edge, so a pentagon base needs 5 rectangles plus 2 pentagon ends, 7 faces in all; a pyramid would show only one pentagon with triangles around it.
